title: Advertisement with URL and No Other Identifying Information
text: A billboard need not show the lawyer’s name, firm, or office address if its web address leads to a site where that information is easy to find.
whatToDo: If an ad shows only a web address, make sure the landing page clearly names the responsible lawyer and office address.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: New York State Bar Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Attorney Newsletters
text: A mainly educational newsletter is not an ad, but a newsletter mainly about the firm’s cases, people or wins is an ad and must follow the ad rules.
whatToDo: Keep newsletters educational, or label and handle them as ads if they mostly promote the firm.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Supreme Court of New Jersey, Advisory Committee on Professional Ethics, Committee on Attorney Advertising, and Committee on the Unauthorized Practice of Law (joint)
title: Lawyers Participating in Impermissible Lawyer Referral Services and Providing Legal Services for Unregistered Legal Service Plans - Avvo, LegalZoom, Rocket Lawyer, and Similar Companies
text: New Jersey lawyers may not join Avvo's legal-services programs, whose per-matter fee is fee-sharing and a paid referral, or unregistered LegalZoom or Rocket Lawyer plans.
whatToDo: Do not join platforms that take a cut of each legal fee or run unregistered legal service plans; flat advertising fees are the safe model.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: North Carolina State Bar (Ethics Committee; adopted by the State Bar Council)
title: Text Message Advertising
text: A lawyer may advertise through a text-message service that lets the user start a live phone call, if the texts follow the ad rules and other laws.
whatToDo: Text ads are allowed, but keep them truthful and comply with federal and state texting laws.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Ohio Board of Professional Conduct
title: Solicitation of Professional Employment Via Email
text: A lawyer may solicit clients by email, and may let a referral or advertising service send it, but the lawyer is responsible for its content.
whatToDo: If you or a vendor send solicitation emails, review the content yourself and follow the solicitation rules.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Philadelphia Bar Association, Professional Guidance Committee
title: A lawyer's right to share legal fees with a referring nonprofit organization whose exclusive purpose is to provide legal services
text: A nonprofit whose only purpose is providing legal services counts as a law firm, so lawyers may share fees with it as a referral fee if Rule 1.5 is met.
whatToDo: You may pay a referral share to a nonprofit legal services group that refers cases, but not to for-profit nonlawyer referrers.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Ohio Board of Professional Conduct
title: Advertisement of Contingent Fee Arrangements
text: A lawyer may not advertise "no fee unless we win" if the client must repay costs regardless of outcome, unless the ad has a disclaimer explaining that duty.
whatToDo: If clients repay case costs no matter what, do not say "no fee unless we win" without a clear cost-repayment disclaimer.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: South Carolina Bar, Ethics Advisory Committee
title: [Advertising "Best Lawyers", "Super Lawyers" and similar designations and badges]
text: A lawyer may advertise an award like Best Lawyers only if the standards are objective and disclosed, the date and source shown, and nothing was paid for it.
whatToDo: Show awards only with the year, the publisher, and a link to the selection standards, and never pay to get the award.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: State Bar of Michigan, Standing Committee on Professional Ethics
title: [Former judge's use of judicial title or image in public communications]
text: A former judge in private practice may not use a judicial title or image that implies current judicial status, though a truthful bio may mention past service.
whatToDo: If a lawyer at your firm is a former judge, say "former" or "retired" and avoid robe or bench images that suggest a sitting judge.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: State Bar of Michigan, Standing Committee on Professional Ethics
title: [Internet domain names and website addresses]
text: Domain names and web addresses are public communications about legal services and must not be false or misleading under MRPC 7.1.
whatToDo: Choose domain names that are truthful and not misleading.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: District of Columbia Bar, Legal Ethics Committee
title: Social Media I: Marketing and Personal Use
text: Promotional social media must follow the ethics rules; lawyers must fix false content on pages they control, answer reviews without confidences, and endorse others only truthfully.
whatToDo: Review the social media pages you control, remove false endorsements, and never reveal client secrets when answering reviews.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Pennsylvania Bar Association, Legal Ethics and Professional Responsibility Committee
title: Settlement Agreements Containing Confidentiality or Non-Disparagement Clauses and Their Effect on Lawyer Marketing for and Representing Future Clients
text: Lawyers may not publicize identifying facts of a client's case in marketing without consent, but may advertise the types of matters they handle.
whatToDo: Get client consent before naming a case or its facts in marketing, and describe practice areas rather than unverifiable win counts against named parties.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Ohio Board of Professional Conduct
title: Client Testimonials in Lawyer Advertising and Online Services
text: Client testimonials are allowed if not misleading, testimonials stating settlement or verdict amounts are misleading, and a lawyer must remove false or misleading reviews on sites the lawyer controls.
whatToDo: Use testimonials with a disclaimer, never quote dollar results in them, and remove misleading reviews from sites you control.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Pennsylvania Bar Association, Legal Ethics and Professional Responsibility Committee
title: Ethical Considerations Relating to Participation in Fixed Fee Limited Scope Legal Services Referral Programs
text: Lawyers may not join Avvo Legal Services-type programs where the company collects the client's fee and takes a marketing fee that rises with it; that is fee-sharing.
whatToDo: Avoid platforms that hold your client's fee or take a percentage-style 'marketing fee'; pay only flat advertising or per-lead costs that do not depend on what you earn.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: State Bar of Texas, Professional Ethics Committee
title: [Using the name of a multi-firm organization (verein) as a Texas firm name]
text: A Texas firm may not use a multi-firm network's name that includes people who were never lawyers in the Texas firm; disclaimers do not cure it.
whatToDo: Do not practice or advertise under a network or affiliation name that lists lawyers who were never in your firm.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: State Bar of Texas, Professional Ethics Committee
title: [Responding publicly to a former client's negative online review]
text: A lawyer may answer a former client's negative online review only with a short, restrained reply that reveals no confidential information.
whatToDo: When you get a bad review, reply briefly without any client details, or do not reply at all.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: State Bar of Wisconsin, Standing Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Advertising and Solicitation in Law-Related Services Owned by Lawyer
text: A lawyer who also runs a financial planning business may mention her law practice in its marketing, but may not offer legal services in person to its clients.
whatToDo: If you own a side business, you may note your law practice in its ads, but do not pitch legal work in person to its customers.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Rhode Island Supreme Court Ethics Advisory Panel
title: [E-mailing members of the Bar to seek client referrals]
text: A firm may e-mail other Rhode Island lawyers asking for referrals; lawyer-to-lawyer e-mails are neither ads nor solicitations, but must still be truthful and follow the specialization rule.
whatToDo: Referral-request e-mails to other lawyers are fine; keep them accurate and avoid improper specialist claims.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: State Bar of Texas, Professional Ethics Committee
title: [Using a competing lawyer's name as a search-engine advertising keyword]
text: Buying a competing lawyer's or firm's name as a search-ad keyword does not by itself break the Texas rules, but the ad text must not be false or misleading.
whatToDo: You may bid on competitor names as keywords in Texas, but keep the ad text truthful and do not imply you are the competitor.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: State Bar of Georgia, Formal Advisory Opinion Board
title: [Sole practitioner firm names using "Group", "Firm" or "& Associates"]
text: A solo lawyer may not use "Group" or "& Associates" in a firm name because they falsely suggest other lawyers, but may use "Firm".
whatToDo: If you practice alone, drop "Group" or "& Associates" from your firm name; "Law Firm" is fine.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Ohio Board of Professional Conduct
title: Lawyer Participation in Referral Services
text: A lawyer may not join an online nonlawyer referral service charging a per-service or percentage 'marketing fee' unless it is registered with the Supreme Court of Ohio.
whatToDo: Before joining an online legal marketplace, check its fee model; avoid per-matter or percentage fees unless it is a registered lawyer referral service.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Supreme Court of New Jersey, Committee on Attorney Advertising
title: Attorney Advertising of Awards, Honors, and Accolades That Compare a Lawyer's Services to Other Lawyers' Services - Reminder From the Committee on Attorney Advertising
text: Comparative awards may be advertised only if the issuer really looked into the lawyer's fitness, with the methodology, issuer name and the Supreme Court disclaimer.
whatToDo: Follow the 2021 reminder, which repeats and expands this notice.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Oregon State Bar, Board of Governors (Legal Ethics Committee)
title: Information about Legal Services: Firm Names—Retired Partner Mediator
text: A firm may keep a retired partner's name in the firm name and list the retired partner as available only as a mediator, if that is not false or misleading.
whatToDo: Keeping a retired partner's name is fine if you state accurately what that person now does.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: State Bar of Texas, Professional Ethics Committee
title: [Offering free bail bond and warrant information to attract visitors to a law office]
text: A lawyer may advertise and give free bail-bond and warrant-check information to office visitors; it is not paying to solicit, but the offer must be honored.
whatToDo: If you advertise free information, give it to everyone who asks, never make it depend on hiring you, and supervise staff who hand it out.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Maryland State Bar Association, Committee on Ethics
title: [Online fixed-fee legal services programs and per-service "marketing" fees]
text: Paying an online fixed-fee legal services company a 'marketing' fee that is charged only when a client hires you and varies with the service is improper fee-sharing with a nonlawyer.
whatToDo: Avoid platforms that charge a per-matter fee that rises with your legal fee; flat advertising fees are allowed.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Maryland State Bar Association, Committee on Ethics
title: Whether a lawyer can pay a fee to an online legal directory for increased visibility throughout the website, including on other lawyers' profile pages?
text: A lawyer may pay an online directory for extra visibility, including ads on other lawyers' profiles, if the ads are truthful and fees are not tied to successful referrals.
whatToDo: Paid directory upgrades are fine if the price is not tied to signed clients; keep your profile accurate.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: South Carolina Bar, Ethics Advisory Committee
title: [Fixed-fee referral service run by an attorney directory website; per-service marketing fee]
text: A lawyer may not join a directory's fixed-fee service that collects the client's fee and keeps a per-service marketing fee; that splits fees and pays for referrals.
whatToDo: Do not join platforms that hold your client’s fee or take a cut that varies by the service you perform.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: State Bar of California, Standing Committee on Professional Responsibility and Conduct (COPRAC)
title: Attorney Blogging
text: A blog is advertising when it is on the firm website or invites readers to hire the lawyer; a stand-alone blog is not unless it signals availability for hire.
whatToDo: Treat any blog on your firm site, or any blog post that invites readers to hire you or details case results, as an ad that must follow the advertising rules.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Washington State Bar Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Ethical Practices of the Virtual or Hybrid Law Office
text: A virtual lawyer may list an accurate P.O. box or business-center address in ads, but may not imply a firm or local office that does not exist.
whatToDo: Use an accurate address in ads and say if you do not meet clients in person there.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Rhode Island Supreme Court Ethics Advisory Panel
title: [Advertising slogan "Win with [lawyer's name]"]
text: Rhyming slogans like 'Win with [name]' are not false or misleading because a reasonable person would not read them as promising to win every case.
whatToDo: Short upbeat slogans are allowed, but pair them with a results disclaimer and do not promise outcomes.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: State Bar of Texas, Professional Ethics Committee
title: [Website email links and warnings to prospective clients about confidentiality]
text: A Texas firm need not post a no-confidentiality warning on website email links, but without an accepted warning it may have to treat what prospects send as confidential.
whatToDo: Put a clear click-to-accept notice before your website contact form or email link if you want to be free to use unsolicited information.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Utah State Bar, Ethics Advisory Opinion Committee
title: [Paying an internet service a nominal fee to bid on legal work]
text: A Utah lawyer may pay a small per-bid fee to an online service to bid on legal work, if conflicts are checked and prospects' information is kept confidential.
whatToDo: You may use pay-per-bid sites, but run a conflict check and protect what prospective clients tell you.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: West Virginia Lawyer Disciplinary Board
title: Social Media and Attorneys
text: Lawyers may advertise on social media but must follow the same rules as elsewhere, must not solicit by real-time electronic contact, and may form prospective-client relationships online.
whatToDo: Treat social media posts and messages like any other ad, avoid real-time solicitation, and use warnings when inviting people to share case details.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Oregon State Bar, Board of Governors (Legal Ethics Committee)
title: Information about Legal Services: Dual Professions, Yellow Pages Advertising
text: A lawyer-mediator may also advertise under a counselors heading if the ad is not misleading and shows the lawyer's status as a lawyer offering mediation.
whatToDo: When you advertise under a non-legal category, say clearly that you are a lawyer.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Oregon State Bar, Board of Governors (Legal Ethics Committee)
title: Information about Legal Services: Insurer-Employed Lawyers' Firm Name
text: Insurance-company staff lawyers may not use a name like 'A & B, Attorneys at Law' without disclosing they are employees of the insurer.
whatToDo: If you are staff counsel, show your employer relationship on letterhead and pleadings.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Illinois State Bar Association, Professional Conduct Advisory Opinions
title: Links on a lawyer's website to other businesses or organizations
text: A law firm's website may include links to other businesses or organizations.
whatToDo: You may link to other businesses on your site, but keep the overall site truthful.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Connecticut Bar Association, Standing Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Lawyer's Participation in a Barter-Exchange Program
text: A lawyer may join a barter exchange with uniform membership and transaction fees, but must make sure its listings and solicitations follow the advertising rules.
whatToDo: If you list on a barter or member network, check that its ads about you are accurate, name your licensing states, and that it does not solicit in person for you.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: District of Columbia Bar, Legal Ethics Committee
title: Sharing of Legal Fees With a Lawyer Referral Service
text: A lawyer may pay a referral service a flat fee per referral, but a percentage only to a qualifying nonprofit or as a true lawyer referral service's usual charge.
whatToDo: Pay referral services flat fees; pay a percentage only to a qualifying nonprofit lawyer referral service.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: North Carolina State Bar (Ethics Committee; adopted by the State Bar Council)
title: Offering Prospective Client a Computer Tablet in Direct Mail Solicitation
text: A lawyer may not offer a free computer tablet to prospective clients in a direct-mail solicitation letter.
whatToDo: Do not offer gifts or prizes to people in solicitation letters.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: New York State Bar Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Compensating clients to rate lawyer on Internet website
text: A lawyer may give clients a $50 bill credit for rating the lawyer on a site like Avvo if the credit does not depend on what they write.
whatToDo: Any reward for a review must be the same whatever the review says, and clients must write it themselves.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Disciplinary Board of the Hawai'i Supreme Court
title: Attorney Web Sites and Other Electronic Advertising
text: Website content, domain names, web and email addresses, banners and pop-ups are advertising and must follow the Hawaii advertising rules.
whatToDo: Treat your website, domain name and online ads as advertising and check them against HRPC 7.1-7.5.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Disciplinary Board of the Hawai'i Supreme Court
title: Captive Law Firms
text: An insurance-company staff lawyer may not use a firm name, letterhead or business card that suggests an independent law firm.
whatToDo: If you are insurer staff counsel, make your employment status clear on all names and letterhead.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Disciplinary Board of the Hawai'i Supreme Court
title: Of Counsel
text: Lawyers may use 'of counsel' or similar titles on letterhead, cards and ads only for a continuing, close and regular relationship, and must state any jurisdiction limits.
whatToDo: Use 'of counsel' only for a real ongoing relationship and note licensing limits.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Disciplinary Board of the Hawai'i Supreme Court
title: Sharing Office Space
text: A lawyer may share office space and staff with nonlawyers if the businesses stay distinct to the public and the nonlawyer does not solicit or feed cases to the lawyer.
whatToDo: If you share space with non-lawyers, keep separate identities and never let them steer clients to you.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Disciplinary Board of the Hawai'i Supreme Court
title: Referral Fees
text: A lawyer may not accept a fee from a nonlawyer business for referring a client to it, even with disclosure and consent.
whatToDo: Never take a referral fee from realtors, advisors, medical providers or other vendors you send clients to.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: New York County Lawyers Association, Professional Ethics Committee
title: The ethical implications of attorney profiles on LinkedIn
text: A LinkedIn profile listing only education and jobs is not an ad, but adding practice areas, skills or endorsements likely makes it one; lawyers must remove inaccurate endorsements.
whatToDo: Treat a LinkedIn profile that lists practice areas, skills or endorsements as an ad, and delete endorsements that aren't accurate. New York dropped the set 'Attorney Advertising' label on June 1, 2026.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: New York State Bar Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Solicitation
text: Answering an online request for a lawyer, in the way invited, is advertising, not solicitation; posts seeking plaintiffs are allowed except about a specific incident during the waiting period.
whatToDo: Reply to online requests for a lawyer only in the way the person asked, and treat the reply as an ad.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Supreme Court of New Jersey (on recommendation of the Committee on Attorney Advertising)
title: Amendments to Attorney Advertising Guideline 2
text: Direct-mail solicitations must print 'ADVERTISEMENT' at the top, larger than the text, and on the envelope, which may carry only basic name and address details.
whatToDo: On solicitation letters, print 'ADVERTISEMENT' two font sizes larger than the body text and keep the envelope to names, addresses and that word.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Oregon State Bar, Board of Governors (Legal Ethics Committee)
title: Firm Names: Office Sharing with Separate Practices
text: Lawyers who only share office space may not call themselves associates or of counsel to each other or use a joint name like 'A, B & C, Lawyers'.
whatToDo: Do not use a shared firm-style name or letterhead with office mates who are not truly your firm.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Oregon State Bar, Board of Governors (Legal Ethics Committee)
title: Information about Legal Services: Multistate Law Firm, Advertising Availability of Out-of-State Lawyer
text: A multistate firm may advertise its out-of-state lawyers to Oregon clients but may not suggest they are Oregon bar members when they are not.
whatToDo: List each lawyer's licensing states accurately on your website and ads.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Colorado Bar Association, Ethics Committee
title: Ethical Responsibilities of Lawyers Who Engage in Other Businesses
text: If a lawyer's side business is not kept clearly separate from the practice, its ads and solicitations must follow the lawyer advertising rules.
whatToDo: Market any side business under its own name, website and ads, with clear disclaimers, or follow the lawyer ad and solicitation rules for it.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Utah State Bar, Ethics Advisory Opinion Committee
title: [Attorney rating systems: 'Best Lawyer' / 'Super Lawyer']
text: A lawyer may advertise a rating only if the rater checked fitness, nothing was paid, the method is public, and the ad says 'included in', not 'the best'.
whatToDo: Say 'named to' a ranking, never 'the best lawyer'; never pay for a rating itself; link to how the rating is chosen.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: New York State Bar Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Responding to a former client’s critical commentary on a website
text: A lawyer may not reveal a former client’s confidential information just to answer that client’s criticism on a lawyer-rating website.
whatToDo: Answer bad reviews without revealing anything confidential about the client.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Pennsylvania Bar Association, Legal Ethics and Professional Responsibility Committee
title: Ethical Obligations for Attorneys Using Social Media
text: Lawyers may use social media, accept and answer reviews if they monitor accuracy, and give or ask for endorsements; practice-promoting posts are subject to the ethics rules.
whatToDo: Monitor reviews and endorsements on your profiles, correct inaccurate ones, and treat any practice-related social media post as lawyer advertising.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: New Hampshire Bar Association, Ethics Committee
title: Providing Discounted Legal Services Through "Group Coupon" or "Daily Deal" Services
text: A lawyer may offer discounted services through a group-coupon site's 'coupon deal' if ethical concerns are handled, but a prepaid voucher deal is unlikely to comply.
whatToDo: If you use Groupon-type promotions, sell only a discount coupon (client pays you later), not a prepaid voucher for legal services.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: State Bar of Michigan, Standing Committee on Professional Ethics
title: [Coupon-type (daily deal) marketing of legal services]
text: Selling legal services through a coupon company that keeps part of the price is improper fee sharing with a nonlawyer.
whatToDo: Do not sell your services through daily-deal coupon sites that take a cut of the fee.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Bar Association of San Francisco, Legal Ethics Committee
title: [Responding to a negative online review by a former client]
text: A lawyer may respond generally to a former client's online review once the matter is over, without confidential information; if it is still open, a substantive reply may be inappropriate.
whatToDo: Answer negative reviews only in general terms and never share client details.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Pennsylvania Bar Association, Legal Ethics and Professional Responsibility Committee
title: Lawyer's Response to Client's Negative Online Review
text: A lawyer may not reveal client confidential information when answering a negative online review without the client's informed consent; any reply should be short and restrained.
whatToDo: Reply to bad reviews, if at all, with a brief note that confidentiality prevents a point-by-point answer, and never share case details.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Vermont Bar Association (advisory ethics opinions; committee name not shown on the opinion)
title: [Paid listing in an accident smartphone app that shows nearby injury lawyers]
text: A firm may buy a geographic listing in a car-accident app showing nearby injury lawyers, since the app recommends no lawyer, if later contact follows the solicitation rules.
whatToDo: Paid directory or app listings sold by area are fine if the vendor does not pick or recommend you; keep any follow-up contact within the solicitation rules.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Washington State Bar Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Participation in online lead generation services
text: A lawyer may pay an internet lead generator flat, monthly or per-click fees if it does not vouch for the lawyer and matches on disclosed objective criteria.
whatToDo: Use lead services that match on objective criteria and do not vouch for you; avoid ones that pick lawyers for clients.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: State Bar of Nevada, Standing Committees on Lawyer Advertising
title: Lawyer Advertising Interpretive Guidelines
text: Past results need a disclaimer and must reflect money the client received; actors and dramatizations must be labeled; only certified specialists may say 'specialist' or 'expert'.
whatToDo: Before running a Nevada ad, check it against these guidelines: label actors and dramatizations, add past-results disclaimers, and do not call yourself a specialist unless certified.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Colorado Bar Association, Ethics Committee
title: Referral Fees and Networking Organizations
text: A Colorado lawyer may not pay referral fees, but may pay a nonprofit referral service's usual charges and join cooperative marketing that is not a disguised referral service.
whatToDo: Do not pay for referrals; check that any marketing vendor or networking group is advertising, not a disguised paid referral service.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Connecticut Bar Association, Professional Ethics Committee
title: Use of a Call Recording Service
text: A lawyer may use a pay-per-call service that records prospective-client calls only if the vendor cannot access the recordings and no third party hears them without consent.
whatToDo: If your call-tracking vendor records intake calls, get a contract term that the vendor cannot access recordings, and limit who can listen.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Los Angeles County Bar Association, Professional Responsibility and Ethics Committee
title: Ethical Duties of Lawyers in Connection with Adverse Comments Published by a Former Client
text: A lawyer may reply publicly to a former client's negative online comment only if the reply reveals no confidences, does not harm the client, and stays restrained.
whatToDo: Reply to bad reviews briefly and politely without revealing anything about the client's matter.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: North Carolina State Bar (Ethics Committee; adopted by the State Bar Council)
title: Use of Search Engine Company's Keyword Advertisements
text: It is dishonest, and a rules violation, for a lawyer to buy another lawyer’s name as a keyword to trigger the lawyer’s own search ads.
whatToDo: Do not bid on any competing lawyer’s name in search-ad campaigns in North Carolina.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Connecticut Bar Association, Professional Ethics Committee
title: Martindale.com Client Review Ratings
text: A lawyer may send clients to rate him on Martindale.com; client-written reviews are not the lawyer's ad unless the lawyer shapes or answers them.
whatToDo: You may ask clients for reviews on third-party sites, but do not write or edit them, and make sure any response you post is accurate.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Vermont Bar Association (advisory ethics opinions; committee name not shown on the opinion)
title: [Shared marketing agreement with a realtor and lender]
text: A lawyer may split ad costs with realtors or lenders if payments cover only real marketing costs, the ads imply no partnership, and referrals follow the reciprocal-referral rules.
whatToDo: In co-marketing deals, pay only your fair share of actual ad costs, review the ad content, and never suggest you are in business with the partner.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: State Bar of California, Standing Committee on Professional Responsibility and Conduct (COPRAC)
title: Social Networking
text: A lawyer's social media posts are advertising when they offer the lawyer's services, such as posting wins and inviting calls, and the ad rules still apply.
whatToDo: Assume posts that mention wins or invite people to hire you are ads; add any required disclaimers and keep them truthful.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Virginia State Bar, Standing Committee on Legal Ethics
title: Is it ethical for a lawyer to become a member of a lead-sharing organization?
text: A lawyer may not join a lead-sharing group, such as a networking club, where membership depends on giving members referrals.
whatToDo: Avoid networking groups that require you to pass a quota of client leads; general professional networking is fine.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Colorado Bar Association, Ethics Committee
title: The Applicability of Colo. RPC 7.2 to Internet-Based Lawyer Marketing Programs
text: A lawyer may pay for an online directory that says it is advertising and charges fixed fees, but not a service that recommends lawyers or charges per client hired.
whatToDo: Before joining an online lead or listing service, confirm it is a neutral, labeled directory with a flat fee, not a paid 'referral' that picks lawyers for clients.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Minnesota Lawyers Professional Responsibility Board
title: Use of the Word “Associates” in a Law Firm Name
text: Using "Associates" in a firm name is misleading unless at least two lawyers practice there, and "& Associates" needs at least three.
whatToDo: Drop "Associates" or "& Associates" from your firm name unless you have enough practicing lawyers to back it up.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Alaska Bar Association, Ethics Committee (adopted by Board of Governors)
title: Use of Membership in Lawyer Ranking System In Lawyer/Law Firm Advertising
text: Lawyers may mention Super Lawyers, Best Lawyers or similar rankings in ads only in a set format that gives the publication name, date, and practice area.
whatToDo: Write ranking claims as 'Name was selected for inclusion in [Publication] [Year] in [practice area]'.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Delaware State Bar Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
title: [Compensation of a law firm's nonlawyer marketing professional]
text: A firm may not pay its nonlawyer marketing employee bonuses calculated as a percentage of firm revenues or of revenue from clients the marketer brings in.
whatToDo: Pay marketing staff and vendors salary or flat fees, not a percentage of the fees they bring in.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Virginia State Bar, Standing Committee on Legal Ethics
title: Obligations of a Lawyer Who Receives Confidential Information Via Law Firm Website or Telephone Voicemail
text: Listing an email or phone does not invite secrets, but a website form asking for case details can create duties, so firms should use a clear click-through disclaimer.
whatToDo: If your website intake form asks for case facts, make visitors click to accept a plain disclaimer saying no lawyer-client relationship or confidentiality is created before they submit.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Delaware State Bar Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
title: [Advertising "Super Lawyer" and "Best Lawyer" designations]
text: A lawyer may advertise being named a 'Super Lawyer' or 'Best Lawyer' if the ad states the year and practice area of the designation and otherwise follows the advertising rules.
whatToDo: When you show a Super Lawyers or Best Lawyers badge, state the year and the practice area it covers.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: District of Columbia Bar, Legal Ethics Committee
title: Participation in Internet-Based Lawyer Referral Services Requiring Payment of Fees
text: Lawyers may join online referral services charging flat participation, per-name or per-client fees, if the fee is not a share of legal fees and listings are not misleading.
whatToDo: Pay online referral or lead services only flat fees, never a share of your legal fee, and check what they say about you.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Oregon State Bar, Board of Governors (Legal Ethics Committee)
title: Internet Advertising: Payment of Referral Fees
text: The Oregon State Bar withdrew this internet-advertising referral-fee opinion in 2018; its text is no longer published.
whatToDo: Do not rely on this opinion; check current RPC 7.2 and later opinions instead.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: State Bar of Texas, Professional Ethics Committee
title: [Paying to join an internet service that forwards potential clients' information to paying lawyers]
text: A Texas lawyer may pay an online service that forwards potential clients' problems to paying lawyers only if it meets the opinion's conditions, which the lawyer keeps checking.
whatToDo: Before buying leads from an online service, confirm it does not pick lawyers for clients, charges a reasonable advertising fee, does not cap participants, and label your first contact as advertising.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: District of Columbia Bar, Legal Ethics Committee
title: Firm Names for Solo Practitioners
text: A solo lawyer may use any trade name that is not false or misleading, and using the word "firm" is not misleading by itself.
whatToDo: Choose a firm name that does not mislead clients about the size or nature of your practice.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Virginia State Bar, Standing Committee on Lawyer Advertising and Solicitation (former); approved by the Supreme Court of Virginia
title: Communications to the Public Involving a Lawyer's Recognition by a Listing in a Publication such as The Best Lawyers in America
text: A lawyer may advertise a truthful Best Lawyers-type listing, but may not claim to be 'the best', credit the whole firm, or tout a credential anyone can buy.
whatToDo: Name the exact listing and year, describe it in plain words, and do not turn one lawyer's listing into a firm-wide 'best' claim.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: State Bar of California, Standing Committee on Professional Responsibility and Conduct (COPRAC)
title: Implied Formation Through Communications Sent via Website
text: A lawyer inviting website questions owes confidentiality unless a plain-language disclaimer defeats visitors' reasonable belief; a bare 'no attorney-client relationship' click-through is not enough.
whatToDo: Put a clear, plain-English warning on web intake forms that what visitors send will not be kept confidential (if that is your policy), not just 'no attorney-client relationship.'
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Oregon State Bar, Board of Governors (Legal Ethics Committee)
title: Information about Legal Services: Initiating Contact with Lawyer-Referral Service Clients
text: The Oregon State Bar withdrew this opinion on lawyers contacting referral-service clients in 2018; its text is no longer published.
whatToDo: Do not rely on this opinion; check current RPC 7.3 instead.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Oklahoma Bar Association, Legal Ethics Committee
title: [Listing jury verdict and settlement amounts in advertising]
text: Ads may state verdict or settlement amounts if accurate and not confidential, with an equally prominent disclaimer that each case is different.
whatToDo: Before advertising a verdict or settlement, make sure it does not reveal client confidences, check the figure, and add an equally prominent 'each case is different' disclaimer.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Kentucky Attorneys' Advertising Commission
title: False, Deceptive and Misleading Advertising
text: The Commission's regulation lists ad content it may treat as misleading, including actors posing as clients, misleading area codes, and verdict amounts without the case facts.
whatToDo: In Kentucky ads, do not show verdict amounts without the case facts, do not let actors look like real clients, and disclose where your office really is.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Kentucky Attorneys' Advertising Commission
title: Advertising of Fees
text: A 'no fee unless we win' ad must say the client may owe costs, and a stated contingent-fee percentage must say whether it is before or after costs.
whatToDo: Next to any 'no fee unless you win' line, add that clients may owe costs and expenses, and say how the percentage is calculated.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: State Bar of Texas, Professional Ethics Committee
title: Ethical Issues Raised by a Lawyer's Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in the Practice of Law
text: Texas lawyers may use generative AI if they understand it, check its output and protect client secrets; an hourly lawyer may charge for time actually spent, not time the tool saved.
whatToDo: If AI helps with client work, check its output, keep client secrets out of tools that learn from inputs, and bill only the time you really spent.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: New York City Bar Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Ethical Obligations of Lawyers and Law Firms Relating to the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in the Practice of Law
topics: ai; ai-tools; advertising-general; solicitation; chatbots; client-intake
text: A lawyer must not use generative AI to dodge the marketing and solicitation rules: no false statements, no AI-driven prohibited solicitations, and no posing as a real person.
whatToDo: Supervise any AI intake chatbot closely, make it say it is not a lawyer, and never use AI to send solicitations the rules forbid.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: American Bar Association, Standing Committee on Ethics and Professional Responsibility
title: Generative Artificial Intelligence Tools
text: The ABA's generative AI opinion covers competence, confidentiality, fees and supervision, and notes only in passing that Model Rule 7.1 on communications may raise more issues.
whatToDo: Treat AI use as covered by the usual duties, and watch for extra issues under Rule 7.1 when AI touches what you say about your services.
confidenceBasis: secondary, non-official source

body: Pennsylvania Bar Association Committee on Legal Ethics and Professional Responsibility and Philadelphia Bar Association Professional Guidance Committee (joint)
title: Ethical Issues Regarding the Use of Artificial Intelligence
text: Pennsylvania lawyers may use AI with competence, confidentiality, verified output and reasonable, disclosed AI expenses; its only advertising line restates Florida's opinion.
whatToDo: Make sure any AI cost you pass on is reasonable and disclosed to the client, and check what AI produces before it goes out.
confidenceBasis: secondary, non-official source

body: District of Columbia Bar, Legal Ethics Committee
title: Attorneys' Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Client Matters
text: D.C. lawyers may use generative AI with the same duties as any tool; an hourly lawyer may bill only the time actually spent, even when AI shortens the work.
whatToDo: Bill hourly work at the time you actually spend, and do not charge extra for AI unless the client agreed in advance.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Kentucky Bar Association, Ethics Committee (adopted by the Board of Governors)
title: The Ethical Use of Artificial Intelligence in the Practice of Law
text: Kentucky lawyers may use AI with competence, supervision and client consent where needed, and should cut the fee when AI cuts the work; the opinion leaves the advertising rules out.
whatToDo: If AI shortens a matter, consider lowering the fee; ask the client before passing on AI costs; and check Kentucky's advertising rules separately for any AI claim in your ads.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: North Carolina State Bar (Ethics Committee; adopted by the State Bar Council)
title: Use of Artificial Intelligence in a Law Practice
text: North Carolina lawyers may use AI if they do so securely and keep independent judgment; a lawyer may not bill for time that AI saved.
whatToDo: Review everything AI produces, keep client information secure, and bill only the work actually done.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: State Bar of Michigan, Standing Committee on Professional Ethics
title: [For-profit online matching services and percentage marketing fees]
text: A for-profit matching service that holds the lawyer's fee and takes a percentage is a barred referral service and fee split, even if it calls that a marketing fee.
whatToDo: Pay for advertising on the ad's value, never as a share of the fee or for each client signed, and keep client funds in your own trust account.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: Illinois State Bar Association, Professional Conduct Advisory Opinions
title: Third party vendor lawyer promotion (advertising) and compensation
text: A firm may not pay a marketing company based on fees from clients it sends; only a lawyer may decide whether someone answering an ad has a claim.
whatToDo: Keep vendor pay apart from case fees, let a vendor turn away only matters in a different field, and read this with the Rule 7.2 in effect since July 2025.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check

body: South Carolina Bar, Ethics Advisory Committee
title: [Co-counseling with or owning part of an alternative business structure]
text: A South Carolina lawyer may not co-counsel with or own part of an alternative business structure with nonlawyer owners, or one that pays nonlawyers who refer clients.
whatToDo: Before taking injury cases from an out-of-state firm that advertises nationally, ask who owns it and where the fee goes; decline if nonlawyers share it.
confidenceBasis: one primary source, no second check
